paper_1: Language-Guided Temporal Token Pruning for Efﬁcient VideoLLM Processing Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 Vision Language Models (VLMs) face signiﬁ- 002 cant computational challenges with long-form 003 videos due to attention mechanisms’ quadratic 004 complexity. We propose Language-Guided 005 Temporal Token Pruning (LGTTP), which ex- 006 tracts temporal cues from queries to adap- 007 tively assign pruning rates across video frames, 008 preserving contextual continuity while reduc- 009 ing computational overhead. Unlike existing 010 methods that apply uniform token pruning or 011 disruptive keyframe selection, LGTTP main- 012 tains higher token density in temporally rele- 013 vant segments. Our model-agnostic approach 014 integrates with TimeChat and LLaVA-Video 015 architectures, demonstrating substantial efﬁ- 016 ciency gains across diverse benchmarks. Ex- 017 periments show LGTTP reduces computation 018 by 65% while preserving 97-99% of orig- 019 inal performance. On highlight detection, 020 LGTTP achieves +9.5% HIT@1 on QVHigh- 021 lights compared to baseline methods, and 022 for temporal grounding, it maintains 99.6% 023 of original R@1 on Charades-STA. LGTTP 024 shows particular strength for queries with ex- 025 plicit temporal markers while remaining effec- 026 tive for general video understanding tasks. 027 1 Introduction 028 Vision Language Models like TimeChat (Ren 029 et al., 2024), LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024), 030 and VideoLLaVA (Lin et al., 2023) have demon- 031 strated exceptional capabilities across various 032 video understanding tasks, from highlight detec- 033 tion to temporal grounding and video question an- 034 swering. However, these models face substantial 035 computational inefﬁciency when processing long- 036 form videos, as they typically encode every frame 037 into visual tokens and process the entire token se- 038 quence for each query. The computational com- 039 plexity grows quadratically with sequence length 040 due to the attention mechanism, making efﬁcient 041 token management a critical challenge for practi- 042 cal deployment. Real-world video queries often 043 target speciﬁc temporal segments, making full se- 044 quence processing inefﬁcient. 045 Current efﬁciency approaches fall into two cat- 046 egories with signiﬁcant limitations: (1) vision to- 047 ken pruning methods like PruMerge (Shang et al., 048 2024) and ToMe (Bolya et al., 2023), which re- 049 duce spatial redundancy within individual frames 050 but fail to capture temporal connections; and (2) 051 keyframe selection methods like KeyVideoLLM 052 (Liang et al., 2024) and VideoTree (Wang et al., 053 2024), which disrupt temporal context by com- 054 pletely discarding intermediate frames. These lim- 055 itations are particularly problematic for temporal 056 understanding tasks that rely on maintaining tem- 057 poral coherence across frames, such as highlight 058 detection and temporal grounding. 059 We propose Language-Guided Temporal Token 060 Pruning (LGTTP), a model-agnostic approach that 061 addresses these limitations by adaptively assign- 062 ing pruning rates based on temporal cues extracted 063 from queries. LGTTP integrates effectively with 064 both TimeChat and LLaVA-Video architectures, 065 showing particular strength with models that have 066 built-in temporal awareness. By leveraging tem- 067 poral elements, LGTTP preserves tokens most rel- 068 evant to temporal queries while reducing compu- 069 tational requirements by 65% and maintaining 97- 070 99% of original performance. 071 Speciﬁcally, our contributions include: (i) A 072 model-agnostic framework that extracts temporal 073 cues from natural language queries to guide to- 074 ken pruning decisions. (ii) A method to inte- 075 grate LGTTP with TimeChat and LLaVA-Video 076 architectures, with particular optimization for 077 temporally-aware models. (iii) Comprehensive 078 evaluation across multiple video understanding 079 benchmarks, demonstrating that LGTTP main- 080 tains near-original performance while signiﬁcantly 081 reducing computational requirements for diverse 082 tasks. 083 1 2 Method 084 Overview and Motivation. LGTTP addresses a 085 fundamental efﬁciency challenge in VideoLLMs: 086 not all frames are equally relevant to a given 087 query, particularly for temporal understanding 088 tasks. While existing approaches either prune to- 089 kens uniformly or select entire keyframes, LGTTP 090 adaptively preserves the most temporally rele- 091 vant tokens while maintaining contextual continu- 092 ity. Our approach consists of three components: 093 temporal cue extraction from queries, temporally- 094 aware relevance prediction for different models, 095 and adaptive token pruning based on predicted 096 relevance. By leveraging temporal indicators in 097 queries, we can concentrate computational re- 098 sources on the most relevant segments. 099 Temporal Cue Extraction. Natural language 100 queries often contain rich temporal information 101 that guides our pruning strategy. Given a query 102 Q, we extract temporal information through two 103 stages: First, we identify temporal markers (e.g., 104 “before," “after," “during") using pattern matching 105 and a ﬁne-tuned classiﬁer, categorizing them into 106 Precedence, Subsequence, or Co-occurrence rela- 107 tionships. Second, we extract reference events and 108 their potential temporal positions - for example, 109 from “after talking to the coach," we identify “talk- 110 ing to the coach" as occurring earlier in the video. 111 This temporal knowledge helps prioritize frames 112 likely to contain moments of interest. 113 Adaptation to VideoLLM Architectures. 114 LGTTP integrates with various VideoLLM archi- 115 tectures according to their temporal awareness 116 capabilities. For timestamp-aware models like 117 TimeChat, we leverage existing timestamp bind- 118 ings where frame embeddings E = {e1, ..., eN} 119 already incorporate timestamp information. For 120 models using temporal instructions (e.g., LLaVA- 121 Video), we add lightweight temporal position 122 embeddings based on normalized frame positions. 123 For standard VLMs without explicit temporal 124 awareness, we introduce a temporal adapter that 125 projects frame indices into a positional embedding 126 space. 127 After adaptation, we compute relevance scores 128 by processing the query embedding eq = Ftext(Q) 129 and calculating base relevance Lbase = a · 130 cos_sim(E′, eq) + b, where a and b are learnable 131 parameters. We then incorporate extracted tempo- 132 ral cues through a weighting mechanism Ltemp = 133 Lbase ⊙Wtemp, where Wtemp prioritizes frames 134 based on identiﬁed temporal relationships. 135 Temporally-Adaptive Token Pruning. The ﬁnal 136 step converts temporal relevance scores into frame- 137 speciﬁc pruning rates. The frame-wise pruning 138 rates are computed as: 139 R = (r1, r2, ..., rN) = αN · softmax(Ltemp) (1) 140 where α controls the overall pruning rate and N 141 is the frame count. This ensures the average prun- 142 ing rate across frames is approximately α, while 143 distribution varies based on temporal relevance. 144 Critically, we employ soft selection rather than 145 hard keyframe selection. For each frame, we re- 146 tain: 147 Ti = max(Tmin, ⌈(1 −ri) · Tfull⌉) (2) 148 tokens, where Tmin is the minimum token count 149 (typically 10% of the original count Tfull). This 150 preserves contextual continuity by maintaining 151 some tokens even from less relevant frames. 152 3 Experiments 153 3.1 Experimental Setup 154 Datasets: We evaluate LGTTP across multiple 155 video understanding benchmarks: QVHighlights 156 (Lei et al.) for moment retrieval tasks with human- 157 written natural language queries; Charades-STA 158 (Gao et al., 2017) for temporal grounding that eval- 159 uates the ability to locate speciﬁc activities de- 160 scribed in text; VideoMME (Fu et al., 2024) for 161 comprehensive video question answering that tests 162 general understanding capabilities across diverse 163 scenarios; and EgoSchema (Zhang et al., 2023) 164 for egocentric video understanding with narrative- 165 style queries capturing ﬁrst-person perspectives. 166 Metrics: We use task-speciﬁc evaluation met- 167 rics aligned with standard benchmarks. For 168 highlight detection on QVHighlights, we report 169 mAP and HIT@1. For temporal grounding on 170 Charades-STA, we measure R@1 at IoU thresh- 171 olds of 0.5 and 0.7. This selection allows us 185 to evaluate LGTTP’s effectiveness across models 186 with varying temporal awareness capabilities and 187 parameter scales. 188 Baselines: We compare LGTTP against: Original 189 unmodiﬁed models. Random token sampling, Uni- 190 form pruning methods: PruMerge (Shang et al., 191 2024) and ToMe (Bolya et al., 2023), Keyframe 192 selection: KeyVideoLLM (Liang et al., 2024), 193 KVTP (Liu et al., 2025): A recent state-of-the-art 194 approach for video token pruning. 195 3.2 Results on Video Understanding Tasks 196 Performance on Temporal Tasks. Table 1 197 shows LGTTP’s performance on highlight de- 198 tection (QVHighlights) and temporal grounding 199 (Charades-STA) when integrated with TimeChat. 200 Our approach maintains near-original perfor- 201 mance (within 0.5-0.8%) despite reducing com- 202 putation by 65%. On QVHighlights, LGTTP 203 achieves 21.2% mAP and 43.7% HIT@1, signif- 204 icantly outperforming other efﬁciency methods, 205 including KVTP (34.2% HIT@1). For tempo- 206 ral grounding on Charades-STA, LGTTP achieves 207 46.5% R@1 at IoU=0.5, matching the original 208 model’s performance while using only 35% of the 209 computation. This demonstrates LGTTP’s partic- 210 ular strength in preserving critical temporal rela- 211 tionships when pruning tokens. 212 Performance on General Video Understanding. 213 Table 2 shows LGTTP’s effectiveness when in- 214 tegrated with LLaVA-Video on question answer- 215 ing and egocentric understanding tasks. Notably, 216 LGTTP maintains performance within 0.6-1.1% 217 of the original models across both 7B and 13B 218 variants. On VideoMME, LGTTP achieves 62.0% 219 accuracy with the 7B model, which is effectively 220 on par with the unpruned model (62.6%). This in- 221 dicates that LGTTP’s temporal awareness beneﬁts 222 extend beyond explicit temporal tasks to general 223 video understanding, where maintaining context 224 across frames remains important. 225 Cross-Model Analysis. Our cross-architecture ex- 226 periments reveal that LGTTP provides consistent 227 beneﬁts regardless of the base model, though with 228 varying magnitudes. The largest improvements 229 come when integrated with TimeChat (+9.5% 230 HIT@1 on QVHighlights compared to KVTP), 231 likely because TimeChat’s timestamp-aware ar- 232 chitecture provides more precise temporal infor- 233 mation for LGTTP to leverage. With LLaVA- 234 Video, gains are more modest but still signiﬁcant 235 (+0.8% on VideoMME), showing LGTTP’s effec- 236 tiveness even with standard temporal modeling ap- 237 proaches. 238 Query-Dependent Performance. A key obser- 239 vation is that LGTTP’s advantage varies with 240 query type. For queries with explicit temporal 241 markers like “before/after," LGTTP outperforms 242 KVTP by 7.2% HIT@1 on QVHighlights. For 243 “during/while" markers, the advantage is 5.8%, 244 while for queries without explicit temporal mark- 245 ers, it maintains a 2.3% improvement. This grada- 246 tion conﬁrms our hypothesis that language-guided 247 pruning is most beneﬁcial when temporal relation- 248 ships are explicitly expressed, though it provides 249 beneﬁts across all query types. 250 Efﬁciency-Performance Balance. Across all ex- 251 periments, LGTTP achieves an optimal efﬁciency- 252 performance balance. On highlight detection, it 253 retains 97.7% of the original mAP performance 254 while on temporal grounding it maintains 99.6% 255 of R@1 (IoU=0.5) performance. For video QA 256 tasks, it preserves 99.0% of the accuracy, all 257 while reducing computation by 65%. This makes 258 LGTTP particularly suitable for real-world deploy- 259 ment scenarios where computational resources are 260 constrained. 261 3 Method FLOPs Video Question Answering Egocentric Understanding VideoMME EgoSchema 7B 13B 7B 13B LLaVA-Video (original) 100% 62.6% 69.5% 54.2% 65.8% Random Sampling 35% 58.3% 62.4% 50.7% 60.5% ToMe 38% 58.9% 62.9% 51.5% 61.2% PruMerge 35% 59.8% 64.5% 52.5% 63.1% KeyVideoLLM 40% 51.3% 60.5% 46.8% 55.2% KVTP 35% 61.8% 66.3% 52.4% 63.6% LGTTP (Ours) 35% 62.0% 67.1% 53.1% 64.0% Table 2: Performance on video question answering (VideoMME) and egocentric understanding (EgoSchema) tasks with LLaVA-Video at 65% pruning rate. 3.3 Ablation Studies 262 Temporal Cue Extraction Impact. Removing 263 the temporal cue extraction component signiﬁ- 264 cantly degrades performance, with varying impact 265 across tasks. For highlight detection, we observe 266 a -6.5% reduction in HIT@1 on QVHighlights, 267 while temporal grounding on Charades-STA drops 268 by -5.1% in R@1. Even general video QA tasks 269 see a -1.8% reduction in accuracy, demonstrat- 270 ing that temporal understanding beneﬁts all video 271 tasks to some degree. 272 Architectural Integration Strategies. Our com- 273 parison of different integration approaches reveals 274 that adaptation strategy matters. The lightweight 275 temporal adapter approach outperforms simple po- 276 sition embedding by 2.1% on QVHighlights and 277 1.5% on VideoMME. This suggests that effec- 278 tively modeling temporal relationships requires 279 more sophisticated integration than just positional 280 information, especially for models without built-in 281 temporal awareness. 282 Soft vs. Hard Selection Effects. The difference 283 between soft and hard selection is particularly pro- 284 nounced. When using hard selection (pruning rate 285 = 0 or 1), performance drops signiﬁcantly across 286 all tasks: -9.3% HIT@1 on QVHighlights, -7.6% 287 R@1 on Charades-STA, and -3.5% accuracy on 288 VideoMME. These results strongly validate our de- 289 sign choice to maintain a minimum token thresh- 290 old for all frames, preserving contextual continuity 291 that proves crucial for video understanding. 292 Pruning Method Integration. LGTTP improves 293 all baseline pruning methods, but the magnitude 294 varies. When combined with PruMerge, we see 295 +14.8% HIT@1 improvement on QVHighlights 296 and +8.7% R@1 on Charades-STA. With ToMe, 297 the improvements are +16.4% and +10.3% respec- 298 tively. This demonstrates LGTTP’s versatility as 299 a framework that can enhance existing token re- 300 duction methods by adding temporal awareness to 301 their pruning decisions. 302 4 Limitations 303 Despite LGTTP’s effectiveness, it has several lim- 304 itations: (1) Performance depends on the presence 305 of temporal cues in queries, with reduced bene- 306 ﬁts for queries lacking explicit temporal markers; 307 (2) Our implementation handles basic temporal 308 relationships but struggles with complex reason- 309 ing involving multiple temporal constraints; (3) 310 While the preprocessing overhead is minimal (0.3- 311 0.5% of total inference time), it requires additional 312 computational steps; and (4) Optimal integration 313 requires architecture-speciﬁc adaptations, poten- 314 tially limiting straightforward deployment across 315 all VideoLLM variants. 316 5 Conclusion 317 We presented Language-Guided Temporal Token 318 Pruning (LGTTP), which leverages temporal cues 319 in queries to adaptively prune visual tokens in 320 VideoLLMs. By preserving temporally relevant 321 tokens while maintaining contextual continuity, 322 LGTTP reduces computation by 65% with min- 323 imal performance loss across highlight detec- 324 tion, temporal grounding, and video QA tasks. 325 Our approach demonstrates consistent advantages 326 over existing efﬁciency methods, particularly for 327 temporally complex queries, preserving 97-99% 328 of original performance while achieving up to 329 +9.5% HIT@1 improvements over baseline prun- 330 ing methods. LGTTP enables more practical de- 331 ployment of powerful VideoLLMs for long-form 332 video analysis, making advanced video under- 333 standing more accessible in resource-constrained 334 environments and real-time applications. Future 335 work will focus on handling more complex tem- 336 poral relationships and exploring extensions to 337 emerging multimodal architectures. 338 5 A Appendix 449 B Related Work 450 B.1 Video Language Models 451 Recent advances in video language modeling have 452 produced a variety of architectures with different 453 approaches to temporal understanding. TimeChat 454 (Ren et al., 2024) incorporates explicit timestamp 455 awareness by binding visual content with corre- 456 sponding timestamps, enabling accurate temporal 457 localization. LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024) 458 uses a temporal instruction preprompt to inform 459 the LLM about the video sampling process. Vide- 460 oLLaVA (Lin et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024) em- 461 ploys a learnable temporal embedding within the 462 vision encoder. While these models demonstrate 463 strong capabilities, they face computational chal- 464 lenges when processing long videos, particularly 465 for tasks requiring precise temporal understanding. 466 Other approaches like VideoChat (Li et al., 2023), 467 Vid2Seq (Yang et al., 2023), and Video-ChatGPT 468 (Maaz et al., 2024) have also shown promising 469 results in video understanding tasks but typically 470 process frames independently, making them less 471 optimal for capturing ﬁne-grained temporal rela- 472 tionships. 473 B.2 Efﬁciency Approaches for VLMs 474 Several approaches have been proposed to address 475 the computational challenges of vision token pro- 476 cessing in VLMs. Vision token pruning meth- 477 ods like PruMerge (Shang et al., 2024), ToMe 478 (Bolya et al., 2023), FastV (Chen et al., 2024), 479 Vid-TLDR (Choi et al., 2024), and DynamicViT 480 (Rao et al., 2021) focus on reducing token counts 481 based on importance metrics like attention entropy 482 or attention scores. However, these methods typ- 483 ically operate on individual frames without con- 484 sidering temporal context. Keyframe selection 485 methods like KeyVideoLLM (Liang et al., 2024), 486 VideoTree (Wang et al., 2024), and Koala (Tan 487 et al., 2024) identify and retain only the most infor- 488 mative frames, but their hard selection approach 489 disrupts temporal coherence. KVTP (Liu et al., 490 2025) bridges these approaches by using soft se- 491 lection to retain some tokens from less relevant 492 frames, but it doesn’t explicitly leverage temporal 493 cues from queries. 494 B.3 Video Understanding Benchmarks 495 The evaluation of VideoLLMs spans multiple 496 specialized benchmarks. For moment retrieval, 497 QVHighlights (Lei et al.) and Charades-STA 498 (Gao et al., 2017) are commonly used to eval- 499 uate a model’s ability to locate temporal seg- 500 ments matching natural language queries. General 501 video understanding capabilities are assessed on 502 benchmarks like VideoMME (Fu et al., 2024) and 503 EgoSchema (Zhang et al., 2023), which include di- 504 verse question-answering tasks. Step localization 505 is evaluated on datasets like NeXT-QA (Xiao et al., 506 2021) and COIN (Yansong Tang, 2019). Our ap- 507 proach aims to improve efﬁciency across this di- 508 verse range of tasks without compromising perfor- 509 mance. 510 C Implementation Details 511 We implement LGTTP by integrating it with 512 TimeChat and LLaVA-Video pipelines. For base 513 token pruning, we adopt PruMerge due to its ef- 514 fectiveness in preserving important visual infor- 515 mation, though our approach is compatible with 516 other pruning methods. The computational over- 517 head of our complete pipeline is minimal, adding 518 only 0.3-0.5% to overall inference time while re- 519 ducing computation by 65%. 520 D Temporal Marker Classiﬁcation 521 We develop our temporal marker classiﬁer without 522 manual annotation using a weakly supervised ap- 523 proach. First, we construct a comprehensive lex- 524 icon of temporal markers by extracting common 525 temporal expressions from existing NLP resources 526 (e.g., “before," “after," “during," “while," “when"). 527 We then use rule-based pattern matching to auto- 528 matically identify and classify these markers in 529 5,000 queries from QVHighlights, Charades-STA, 530 and VideoMME training sets. 531 The automatically labeled dataset is used to 532 train a 2-layer MLP classiﬁer on top of frozen 533 BERT embeddings. To improve robustness, we 534 employ data augmentation techniques including 535 synonym replacement and word reordering to cre- 536 ate variations of queries with preserved temporal 537 relationships. We also include queries without ex- 538 plicit markers as negative examples. 539 Our classiﬁer achieves 88.6% accuracy when 540 evaluated against a small manually veriﬁed test set 541 of 200 queries. For queries without explicit mark- 542 ers but containing implicit temporal references 543 6 (e.g., “show the beginning"), we rely on a prede- 544 ﬁned vocabulary of temporal terms and their rela- 545 tive positions in the video timeline. This approach 546 allows us to effectively identify temporal relation- 547 ships without requiring extensive manual annota- 548 tion. 549 7
paper_2: BRSpeech-DF: A Deep Fake Synthetic Speech Dataset for Portuguese Zero-Shot TTS Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 The detection of audio deepfakes (ADD) has 002 become increasingly important due to the rapid 003 evolution of generative speech models. How- 004 ever, progress in this field remains uneven 005 across languages, particularly for low-resource 006 languages like Portuguese, which lack high- 007 quality datasets. In this paper, we intro- 008 duce BRSpeech-DF, the first publicly avail- 009 able ADD dataset for Portuguese, encompass- 010 ing both Brazilian and European variants. The 011 dataset contains over 459,000 utterances, in- 012 cluding a smaller portion of real speech from 62 013 speakers and a large collection of synthetic sam- 014 ples generated using multiple zero-shot text-to- 015 speech (TTS) models, each conditioned on the 016 original speaker’s voice. By providing this re- 017 source, our objective is to support the develop- 018 ment of robust, multilingual detection systems, 019 thereby advancing equity in speech forensics 020 and security research. BRSpeech-DF addresses 021 a significant gap in annotated data for underrep- 022 resented languages, facilitating more inclusive 023 and generalizable advancements in synthetic 024 speech detection. 025 Our dataset and codes are publicly available1. 026 1 Introduction 027 The increasing sophistication of generative mod- 028 els has resulted in a proliferation of highly realis- 029 tic synthetic media (Xie et al., 2025), including 030 speech deepfakes. While such technologies of- 031 fer promising opportunities for accessibility and 032 human-computer interaction, they also pose signifi- 033 cant threats to societal trust, privacy, and security 034 (Kharvi, 2024). The potential for audio deepfakes 035 to be weaponized for impersonation, fraud, and 036 misinformation is particularly concerning in sce- 037 narios where voice-based authentication or content 038 verification plays a critical role. 039 1https://anonymous.4open.science/r/dataset_ df-09D5 Recent breakthroughs in zero-shot TTS have fur- 040 ther lowered the barriers to generating speech in 041 arbitrary voices, requiring only a few seconds of 042 reference audio to convincingly imitate a speaker 043 without any fine-tuning (Li et al., 2024b; Bang and 044 Chun, 2023). These advancements make it increas- 045 ingly easy to generate realistic audio for malicious 046 purposes, raising the urgency for robust audio deep- 047 fake detection (ADD) systems. 048 In parallel, the research community has made 049 notable strides in developing detection techniques 050 for deepfakes, employing both features and deep 051 learning methods to distinguish synthetic from real 052 audio (Delgado et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2025). 053 However, the majority of existing datasets and 054 benchmarks focus on high-resource languages, pri- 055 marily English, creating a linguistic bias in the 056 training and evaluation of detection systems (Li 057 et al., 2024a). 058 Moreover, the combination of zero-shot synthe- 059 sis capabilities and the lack of annotated deepfake 060 corpora in underrepresented languages presents a 061 unique and actual research challenge. Without ap- 062 propriate datasets, it is difficult to assess the effec- 063 tiveness of detection models or develop defenses 064 that are culturally and linguistically inclusive. 065 To address this gap, we introduce BRSpeech- 066 DF, the first publicly available dataset designed for 067 audio deepfake detection in Portuguese. By lever- 068 aging modern zero-shot TTS models to generate 069 high-quality synthetic utterances, paired with corre- 070 sponding real speech samples, our dataset enables 071 the development and evaluation of detection sys- 072 tems in a linguistically diverse setting. We hope 073 this resource will encourage further research on 074 ADD for low-resource languages and foster the cre- 075 ation of more equitable and robust speech security 076 technologies. 077 1 2 Dataset 078 The BRSpeech-DF dataset comprises a total of 079 459.137 audio files in Brazilian and European Por- 080 tuguese, encompassing 160 hours of natural speech 081 and 829 hours of synthetic speech, distributed be- 082 tween 62 real speakers (37 men and 25 women) 083 whose voices were cloned using zero-shot mod- 084 els. For each sentence in the real speech set, syn- 085 thetic versions were generated using all 5 zero-shot 086 models, with the reference speaker’s own voice al- 087 ways maintained. BRSpeech-DF is organized into 088 three mutually exclusive splits - training, validation 089 and test - defined by speaker separation, in order 090 to avoid voice leakage between the sets. The dataset under consider- 098 ation includes recordings in Brazilian Portuguese 099 and European Portuguese, with a sampling rate of 100 48 kHz for both. 101 2.2 Construction of the Synthetic Data 102 Zero-Shot Models Employed. To generate the 103 synthetic versions of each sentence, five zero-shot 104 speech synthesis models were employed: Fish- 105 Speech (Liao et al., 2024), XTTS (Casanova et al., 106 2024), F5-TTS (Chen et al., 2024), YourTTS 107 (Casanova et al., 2022) and ToucanTTS (Lux et al., 108 2024). 109 Each model was configured with its official re- 110 lease, and the original implementations were kept 111 without structural modifications, ensuring compa- 112 rability with literature results. 113 Synthesis Pipeline. The generation of synthetic 114 samples was based directly on the sentences in 115 2https://librivox.org/ the original speech corpus. Initially, all recordings 116 lacking an associated textual transcription were dis- 117 carded, ensuring semantic integrity between audio 118 and text during synthesis. For each remaining real 119 sentence, and for each of the five zero-shot models 120 utilized, cloning was carried out using the original 121 audio itself as the voice reference and the corre- 122 sponding text as the textual input. 123 This procedure ensured that the speaker’s vocal 124 identity was preserved in all synthetic versions of 125 the same sentence, which is essential for creating 126 convincing examples of deepfakes. 127 To ensure consistency in the evaluation pipeline, 128 all audio was standardized to 24 kHz, including 129 resampled outputs from FishSpeech (48 kHz) and 130 YourTTS (16 kHz). 131 2.3 Dataset Analysis 132 Model uTMOS ↑ Spk. We aim to demonstrate two main 182 points: (i) to what extent standard detectors trained 183 on other languages generalize to Brazilian Por- 184 tuguese without retraining, and (ii) why a dedicated 185 Portuguese dataset is valuable for future research. 186 To fairly evaluate these models, we calibrated each 187 detector’s decision threshold using their respective 188 original evaluation datasets. 189 3.1 Experimental Setup 190 For our experiments, we report all results using 191 the test split (see Table 1), while reserving the dev 192 split for future experiments such as fine-tuning. paper_3: From Benchmark to Better Embeddings: Leveraging Synonym Substitution to Enhance Multimodal Models in Ukrainian Anonymous ACL submission Abstract Multimodal retrieval models, such as Open- 001 CLIP, rely on aligned textual and visual rep- 002 resentations, yet their robustness to lexical 003 variations remains underexplored, especially 004 in low-resource languages. In this study, we 005 introduce three methods for generating syn- 006 onym substitutions in Ukrainian: a dictionary- 007 based approach, a large language model (LLM)- 008 generated approach, and a hybrid method com- 009 bining both. We further demonstrate that fine- 010 tuning Open-CLIP with synonym-augmented 011 data improves retrieval robustness, leading to a 012 7% increase in HIT@5. Our findings provide 013 insights into synonym substitution techniques 014 for low-resource languages and offer a path- 015 way to enhancing the robustness of multimodal 016 models in diverse linguistic settings. 017 1 Introduction 018 Multimodal retrieval systems, such as those based 019 on CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), rely on aligning tex- 020 tual and visual representations. An open problem 021 in these systems is ensuring that small linguistic 022 variations—such as synonym substitutions—do not 023 lead to markedly different retrieval outcomes. In an 024 ideal scenario, substituting a word with a synonym 025 would yield the same or similar images; however, 026 biases in training data can cause the model to favor 027 specific synonyms, resulting in inconsistent per- 028 formance. This issue is particularly concerning in 029 low-resource languages, where models have lim- 030 ited exposure to diverse synonymous expressions 031 during training. 032 Recent studies have examined the adversarial ro- 033 bustness of multimodal models. For instance,(Zhou 034 et al., 2024) demonstrated that adversarial perturba- 035 tions in both text and image modalities can degrade 036 performance. Similarly, (Liu, 2024) compared mul- 037 timodal and unimodal models under text-based at- 038 tacks and found that, despite some improvements, 039 multimodal models remain vulnerable to lexical 040 variations. Notably, much of this research has fo- 041 cused on high-resource languages, leaving the ro- 042 bustness of these models in low-resource language 043 contexts relatively underexplored. 044 In this study, we evaluate the robustness of mul- 045 tilingual multimodal models for retrieval tasks in 046 a low-resource language setting using the Open- 047 CLIP (Cherti et al., 2023) model and a Ukrainian 048 version of the Multi30K dataset (Saichyshyna et al., 049 2023). Our contributions are threefold: (i) we estab- 050 lish a baseline for robustness evaluation under syn- 051 onym substitutions for Ukranian language, (ii) we 052 conduct a detailed analysis of model performance 053 under lexical variations using three synonym sub- 054 stitution pipelines—a dictionary-based approach, 055 a large language model approach and hybrid, and 056 (iii) we demonstrate that fine-tuning with synthetic 057 synonym replacements enhances robustness, as evi- 058 denced by an average ~7% increase in HIT@5 after 059 synonym substitution. 060 2 Related Work 061 Multimodal text-to-image models mostly follow 062 the CLIP-like approach (Radford et al., 2021), 063 which enables joint learning of image and text 064 representations. While the original CLIP model 065 was trained monolingually, several successful adap- 066 tations have extended its capabilities to multilin- 067 gual settings. Notable examples include mCLIP 068 (Chen et al., 2023) and Cross-lingual CLIP (Carls- 069 son et al., 2022), which employ a teacher-student 070 transfer learning approach to adapt CLIP to multi- 071 ple languages. Another strategy involves replacing 072 the CLIP text encoder with a multilingual language 073 model and training it on a multilingual dataset, as 074 demonstrated in Open-CLIP (Cherti et al., 2023). 075 We evaluated both approaches on the Ukrainian 076 version of Multi30K and found that Open-CLIP 077 outperformed the teacher-student methods, making 078 it the primary model for our study. 079 1 A widely used method for assessing model ro- 080 bustness involves adversarial attacks, which intro- 081 duce perturbations to test a model’s sensitivity to 082 input variations. In this work, we focus on text- 083 based robustness, specifically in the Ukrainian lan- 084 guage, by evaluating the model’s sensitivity to syn- 085 onym substitutions. Synonym-based adversarial 086 attacks are well-studied in high-resource languages 087 such as English, where various approaches exist 088 to generate semantically and syntactically valid 089 substitutions (Jin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020). How- 090 ever, these methods rely on lexical resources like 091 WordNet or pretrained Counter-fitting embeddings 092 (Mrkši´c et al., 2016), which are not available for 093 low-resource languages like Ukrainian. Further- 094 more, many synonym substitution techniques have 095 been found to generate invalid replacements, as 096 highlighted in (Chiang and Lee, 2023). 097 Given these limitations, instead of directly adapt- 098 ing existing synonym substitution techniques from 099 English, we propose a novel approach leveraging 100 large language models (LLMs) to generate con- 101 textually and grammatically appropriate synonym 102 replacements for Ukrainian. 103 3 Methodology 104 3.1 Problem Defenition 105 We define our primary objective as evaluating and 106 improving the robustness of multimodal embed- 107 dings, specifically Open-CLIP, to synonym substi- 108 tutions in a low-resource, morphologically rich lan- 109 guage setting. Our experiments focus on Ukrainian, 110 using Multi30K as the underlying dataset. 111 First, we establish baseline performance by mea- 112 suring how well Open-CLIP retrieves images us- 113 ing the original English and Ukrainian captions 114 from Multi30K utilizing the key retrieval met- 115 rics—HIT@1, HIT@5, and Mean Reciprocal Rank 116 (MRR)—for both English and Ukrainian test sets. 117 As shown in Table 1, the model achieves a HIT@1 118 of 0.416 and a HIT@5 of 0.657 for English, but 119 these metrics drop to 0.321 and 0.543 for Ukrainian, 120 respectively. These results indicate a performance 121 gap between English and Ukrainian. 122 To assess robustness, we measure how much 123 retrieval accuracy degrades when we apply syn- 124 onym substitutions to the Ukrainian captions. Un- 125 like English, where WordNet and other lexical 126 resources facilitate systematic synonym replace- 127 ments, Ukrainian’s morphological complexity com- 128 plicates this process: valid synonyms must match 129 the grammatical form of the original word to retain 130 meaning. In the following Approach section 3.2, 131 we describe our method for systematically gen- 132 erating Ukrainian synonyms and evaluating their 133 impact on image retrieval performance. 134 To assess robustness, we measure how much re- 135 trieval accuracy degrades when we apply synonym 136 substitutions to the Ukrainian captions. To ensure 137 a clear experimental setup and isolate the effect 138 of synonym substitutions, we evaluate robustness 139 only on a subset of Multi30K where the original 140 model correctly retrieves the image. This approach 141 helps mitigate potential errors from the model or 142 dataset itself, allowing us to focus specifically on 143 the impact of lexical variations. Unlike English, 144 where WordNet and other lexical resources facili- 145 tate systematic synonym replacements, Ukrainian’s 146 morphological complexity complicates this pro- 147 cess: valid synonyms must match the grammatical 148 form of the original word to retain meaning. Unlike En- 157 glish, where words generally appear in a single 158 invariant form, Ukrainian words change with num- 159 ber, gender, and case, making it difficult to preserve 160 semantic equivalence during automated substitu- 161 tion. Furthermore, the lack of modern synonym 162 substitution frameworks exacerbates the challenge 163 of evaluating model robustness. 164 To address these issues, we explore three syn- 165 onym generation approaches. The first method is 166 dictionary-based, using the Словник синонiмiв 167 української мови (Наукова думка, 1999), 168 which contains 9,200 synonym groups. Although 169 this resource offers broad lexical coverage, it 170 is prone to parsing errors, outdated terms, and 171 domain-specific constraints that can result in gram- 172 matical mismatches; therefore, after selecting a 173 2 synonym from the dictionary, we apply Pymorphy 174 to adjust its form to fit the sentence context. 175 The second method leverages a large language 176 model (GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024)) to generate 177 context-aware synonyms that are both semantically 178 and grammatically appropriate. 179 Recognizing the strengths and limitations of both 180 methods, we propose a third method, the hybrid 181 approach in which dictionary candidates are refined 182 by the language model to select synonyms that 183 best maintain sentence meaning and grammatical 184 integrity. 185 Synonym Substitution Method HIT@1 HIT@5 MRR Dictionary 0.206 0.512 0.358 GPT-4o 0.335 0.676 0.49 Hybrid 0.446 0.776 0.593 Table 2: Perfomance of Open-CLIP on Ukrainian Multi30K test set by different synonym substitution methods. It shows that the choice of 188 synonym substitution strategy has a substantial im- 189 pact on retrieval performance. A purely dictionary- 190 based approach yields the lowest scores across all 191 metrics. We attribute this drop in accuracy to the 192 dictionary’s limited contextual awareness: while 193 it offers broad lexical coverage, the synonyms it 194 provides often fail to match the morphological and 195 semantic context of each sentence. 196 In contrast, the GPT-based approach signifi- 197 cantly improves performance by generating syn- 198 onyms that better preserve both meaning and gram- 199 matical form, thereby reducing unintended shifts 200 in the text representation. 201 The best results, however, come from the hybrid 202 method, in which dictionary candidates are refined 203 by a large language model. This combined strategy 204 benefits from the dictionary’s lexical breadth and 205 the LLM’s context sensitivity, leading to more pre- 206 cise synonym matches and higher overall retrieval 207 scores. 208 Despite these gains, further improvements re- 209 main necessary, particularly for morphologically 210 rich and low-resource languages like Ukrainian. 211 3.3 Robustness Enhancement 212 To investigate whether the observed synonym sub- 213 stitution issues are primarily attributable to insuf- 214 ficient training data, we first fine-tune Open-CLIP 215 on the Ukrainian portion of the Multi30K training 216 set. This baseline fine-tuning approach allows us 217 to assess whether additional in-language data alone 218 can narrow the performance gap. 219 However, given the hypothesis that many multi- 220 lingual models are trained on machine-translated 221 data—and thus may inherit biases from automated 222 translation systems—we further expand our train- 223 ing corpus by incorporating sentences with syn- 224 onym substitutions generated through the GPT- 225 based method. By enriching the training set with 226 diverse lexical variants, we aim to strengthen the 227 model’s robustness to subtle linguistic shifts com- 228 monly overlooked in low-resource languages. 229 We keep most Open-CLIP layers frozen to retain 230 general multilingual knowledge, while selectively 231 unfreezing a subset of text and vision layers for 232 targeted adjustments. The precise hyperparameters 233 are detailed in Appendix B. 234 4 Results 235 Table 3 demonstrates that fine-tuning improves per- 236 formance across all synonym substitution meth- 237 ods. For example, under the hybrid approach, 238 HIT@5 increases from 0.776 in the original model 239 to 0.816 after Multi30k fine-tuning, and further 240 to 0.839 with synonym-augmented fine-tuning. 241 This pattern holds across methods: while standard 242 fine-tuning yields noticeable gains, incorporating 243 GPT-generated synonyms during fine-tuning con- 244 sistently results in better performance, particularly 245 as measured by HIT@5. 246 Although fine-tuning on the Multi30K dataset 247 alone does enhance robustness by giving the model 248 more extensive exposure to Ukrainian text, the 249 most substantial gains emerge when we expand 250 the training corpus with diverse synonym substi- 251 tutions. A likely reason is that many less com- 252 mon or informal Ukrainian terms are rare or absent 253 in the original pretraining data. As a result, the 254 model sometimes misaligns text and images when 255 encountering these unfamiliar synonyms. In ad- 256 dition, the model can develop biases associating 257 certain synonyms with specific contexts, causing it 258 to fail when these words appear alongside contra- 259 dictory descriptors.
